werk/yoko-ono-feeling-the-space.text:
Feeling the Space is Yoko Ono's fourth solo album, released in 1973, and her last on Apple Records. The whole album revolves around feminist themes and the problems women faced in the 1970s. The sleeve notes parody adverts for adults: they give telephone numbers, birth dates and measurements of the male band members. John Lennon appears on it as John O'Cean, with the song Not for Sale.

Lennon plays guitar on Woman Power and She Hits Back and sings along on Men, Men, Men. The album was intended as a double album, until EMI and Apple demanded that it be shortened. The musicians include Jim Keltner on drums, Michael Brecker on saxophone and Sneaky Pete Kleinow on pedal steel. On release, Billboard called it her most commercial record to date and praised the melodic songs and the singing.
werk/yoko-ono-feeling-the-space.listen: Listen to Woman Power and notice Lennon's guitar, which here plays along under a pseudonym.

werk/yoko-ono-fly.text:
Yoko Ono made this double album in 1971 together with John Lennon, around the same time as his album Imagine. It was her second album, shortly after the debut Yoko Ono/Plastic Ono Band. She divided the four sides into two kinds of music: songs to dance to, and music to listen to. Lennon brought in musicians such as Jim Keltner and Klaus Voormann.

Mind Train lasts almost seventeen minutes, a conversation between her voice and Lennon's guitar. Mrs. Lennon is the most conventional song, a ballad with Lennon on piano. On side three, Ono plays with self-playing sound machines by the Fluxus musician Joe Jones. The title track takes up almost an entire side: her voice was recorded first, then Lennon added guitar, some of it played backwards. The sleeve was a complete avant-garde package, with a poster and a card for ordering her book Grapefruit. In the American chart the album reached number 199.
werk/yoko-ono-fly.listen: Listen to Mrs. Lennon and notice how ordinary this song sounds: a simple ballad with piano, in contrast to the long experimental pieces on the rest of the album.

werk/zbigniew-preisner-requiem-for-my-fr.text:
Requiem for My Friend is the first work by Zbigniew Preisner that was not written for a film, and immediately a major one. He wrote it in memory of his late friend, the director Krzysztof Kieślowski, with whom he worked on several films, including the Three Colours trilogy. The album was released in 1998. Parts of the work were probably already finished when Kieślowski died in 1996. In an interview the composer said that the requiem had accompanied his friend on his last journey.

The work consists of two parts. The first, Requiem, has Latin sections such as Officium, Kyrie eleison, Dies irae, Sanctus, Agnus Dei, Lux aeterna, Lacrimosa and Epitaphium. The second part, Życie, runs through Początek, Przeznaczenie and Apokalipsa to Postscriptum. Lacrimosa can later be heard in Terrence Malick's The Tree of Life from 2011.
werk/zbigniew-preisner-requiem-for-my-fr.listen: Listen to Lacrimosa, the piece heard in The Tree of Life, and notice the mood it evokes.

werk/zero-7-simple-things.text:
Simple Things is the debut of the English duo Henry Binns and Sam Hardaker, together known as Zero 7. It was released on 23 April 2001 and spent 56 weeks in the UK chart, peaking at number 28. The album was nominated for the Mercury Prize. Five singles had already been released before the album came out, among them Destiny and In the Waiting Line.

The duo combines soul-style vocals, tinkling keyboards and classical string arrangements into a soothing sound. Guest vocalists included Sia Furler, Mozez and Sophie Barker. AllMusic gave it four stars out of five. Rolling Stone called it more jazz on acid than acid jazz, chill-out music with something to think about. Pitchfork felt it resembled Air's Moon Safari too closely. In the Waiting Line was later heard in the film Garden State.
werk/zero-7-simple-things.listen: Listen to In the Waiting Line and notice how the gentle backing gives Sophie Barker's voice all the space it needs.

werk/zoot-sims-the-modern-art-of-jazz.text:
Tenor saxophonist Zoot Sims recorded this album in 1956 for the label Dawn; it was also released under the title One to Blow On. He plays in a quintet with Bob Brookmeyer on valve trombone, John Williams on piano, Milt Hinton on bass and Gus Johnson on drums.

The repertoire consists of standards, such as September in the Rain and Ghost of a Chance, and of pieces by the band members, such as Down at the Loft by pianist Williams and Our Pad by Brookmeyer and Johnson. Sims wrote the remaining pieces himself. The CD reissue has two bonus tracks. AllMusic gave the album four stars and praised the interplay between Sims and Brookmeyer: according to reviewer Ken Dryden, their lines weave seamlessly together.
werk/zoot-sims-the-modern-art-of-jazz.listen: Listen to Them There Eyes and notice how the tenor saxophone and the valve trombone play around each other, complementing each other's lines.
